sections.instructions: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow each passage.

options: The courtyard of her old house
questions.passage: When Meera Kulkarni moved into her fourth-floor flat in Pune, the first thing she missed was the sparrows. In the old house where she had grown up, the birds had been everywhere: on the window ledges, under the eaves, and in the courtyard, where her grandmother scattered grain every morning. In the new housing society, the balconies were neat, the lawns were trimmed, and no bird seemed to live there at all. Meera decided to act. She hung a small earthen bowl of water on her balcony rail and filled a feeder with millet. For three weeks, nothing came. Then, one October morning, she heard a thin, familiar chirp. A single sparrow sat on the rail, tilting its head at the feeder. By the end of the month there were six, and by winter the balcony had become, in her neighbours' words, a small station for birds. Other residents began to copy her. The society's garden committee set aside one wild corner of the grounds where grass was allowed to grow tall and go to seed. A local bird group counted forty-one sparrows in the society that spring, where a year earlier there had been none.
questions.prompt: What did Meera miss most when she moved into the new flat?

options: A nest box and a swing
A bowl of water and a feeder with millet
questions.prompt: What did Meera place on her balcony rail?

scheme.answer: b) A bowl of water and a feeder with millet

questions.prompt: How long did Meera wait before the first sparrow arrived?

options: It planted a row of trees
It left one corner of the grounds wild
It built a pond for birds
questions.prompt: What did the society's garden committee do?

scheme.answer: c) It left one corner of the grounds wild

questions.prompt: How many sparrows did the local bird group count in the society that spring?

questions.passage: Every June, when the first monsoon clouds gathered, the students of Green Valley School watched the rain run off the school roof and disappear down the drains. 'We catch nothing,' said Arif, a Class IX student, during an environmental studies period, 'and by February our taps are dry.' The remark became a project. With their teacher's help, the students measured the roof of the main block and calculated that a single heavy shower could fill three large tanks. They drew plans, priced the pipes and filters, and presented the proposal to the school management, which agreed to pay for the materials if the students did the planning and kept the records. By October, the system was ready. Rain from the roof now passes through a simple leaf filter into two storage tanks. The water is used for the school garden and for flushing, and a painted gauge on the tank wall shows everyone how much has been saved. In its first year, the project collected enough water to keep the garden green through the dry months, and the school's water bill fell by nearly a fifth. The students' record book, with its neat columns of rainfall and tank levels, is now the first thing visitors are shown.
questions.prompt: What problem did Arif point out in his environmental studies period?

value_points: Rain ran off the school roof and was lost down the drains
Nothing of the monsoon water was collected or stored
By February the school taps ran dry

questions.prompt: On what condition did the school management agree to pay for the materials?

value_points: The students must do the planning themselves
The students must keep the records of the project
The management would pay only for materials, not for the planning work

questions.prompt: Through what does the roof water pass before it reaches the tanks, and what two uses is the stored water put to?

value_points: It passes through a simple leaf filter
The water is used for the school garden
The water is also used for flushing

questions.prompt: State any two results of the project in its first year.

value_points: The collected water kept the school garden green through the dry months
The school's water bill fell by nearly a fifth

questions.prompt: Which two details did the students record in their record book?

value_points: The rainfall
The tank levels

sections.title: Reading

sections.instructions: Attempt all questions. Internal choices are given where marked. Keep to the word limits stated.

choice.alternative_prompt: You took part in a tree-plantation drive in your neighbourhood last weekend. Write a diary entry, in about 120 words, recording how the day went and how you felt at the end of it.

questions.prompt: You are the Secretary of the Cultural Society of your school. Your school is holding an inter-house painting competition next month. Write a notice, in about 50 words, informing the students of Classes IX to XII about the competition. Give the date, the venue, and how names are to be registered.

alternative_value_points: Date and time of writing at the top
Events of the day in sequence
A closing note looking back on the day
value_points: Format: name of the school or society, the word NOTICE, and the date
A clear heading naming the competition
Date, time, and venue of the competition
Who may take part (Classes IX to XII) and how and by when to register names
Name and designation of the student issuing the notice

choice.alternative_prompt: Write a letter to the manager of a sports-goods shop, in about 120 words, complaining about a cricket bat that you bought from the shop last month and that cracked within a week of use. Ask for a replacement or a refund.

questions.prompt: Write a letter to the Editor of a local newspaper, in about 120 words, drawing attention to the poor condition of the public park in your area and suggesting two improvements that the authorities could make.

alternative_value_points: Sender's address, date, and the shop's address
Reference to the purchase: item, date, and bill if mentioned
Clear statement of the defect and when it appeared
A firm but polite request for a replacement or refund
value_points: Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject line, salutation and subscription
The present condition of the park stated in concrete detail
Two practical improvements suggested
A request that the authorities act, with the public benefit pointed out

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph, in about 150 words, on the topic: A hobby can teach you things that a classroom cannot.

value_points: A clear opening stand on the topic
At least two supporting points or examples
Points linked in a logical order
A concluding line that rounds off the stand taken

choice.alternative_prompt: Write a descriptive paragraph, in about 150 words, describing a railway station early in the morning.

questions.prompt: Write a short story, in about 150 words, beginning with the line: The old lighthouse keeper climbed the stairs for the last time.

alternative_value_points: The scene set with time and atmosphere
Sensory detail: sounds, sights, and smells of the early morning
People and activity described in an orderly movement across the scene
value_points: The given opening line used and carried forward naturally
A clear sequence of events with a turning point
Character shown through action or feeling, not only described
An ending that grows out of the events

questions.passage:
The River in October

After the rains, the river slows,
And learns the names of stones again;
It carries leaves, a broken oar,
The sky's last light, the smell of rain.
The heron stands where shallows gleam,
One leg, one shadow, perfectly still;
And all the noise of summer seems
To settle softly on the hill.
questions.prompt: What does the river 'learn' again after the rains, and what does the phrase suggest?

value_points: It learns the names of the stones again
The water level falls after the rains, so the stones of the river bed show once more
The phrase suggests the river returning calmly to its familiar, quieter course

questions.prompt: Name any three things that the river carries in the poem.

value_points: Leaves
A broken oar
The sky's last light (or: the smell of rain) - any three of these

questions.prompt: What picture of the heron does the poet create?

value_points: It stands in the shallow water where the light gleams
It stands on one leg, with one shadow, perfectly still
The picture is one of patience and complete calm

questions.passage: Mr Elias had mended clocks in the same small shop for forty years. His hands, once steady enough to hold a screw the size of a grain of rice, now trembled slightly, but his ears had grown sharper with age. 'A clock tells you what is wrong with it,' he would say, 'if you have the patience to listen.' Young Thomas, who came after school to sweep the floor and watch, did not understand this at first. He wanted to open every clock at once. Slowly, though, he learnt to sit still, to wind, to wait, and to hear the small uneven heartbeat inside the brass case. On the day Mr Elias retired, he gave Thomas his own magnifying glass. 'The tools are nothing,' he said. 'The listening is everything.'
questions.prompt: For how long had Mr Elias worked in the shop, and what change had age brought to his hands and to his ears?

value_points: He had mended clocks in the same shop for forty years
His hands now trembled slightly
His ears had grown sharper with age

questions.prompt: What did Thomas want to do at first, and what did he slowly learn to do?

value_points: At first he wanted to open every clock at once
Slowly he learnt to sit still, to wind, to wait, and to listen for the uneven heartbeat inside the case

questions.prompt: What did Mr Elias give Thomas on the day he retired, and what did his parting words mean?

value_points: He gave Thomas his own magnifying glass
His words: 'The tools are nothing. The listening is everything.'
Meaning: real skill lies in patience and attention, not in the instruments

questions.prompt: Thomas changes from an impatient boy into a careful listener. Describe this change, and say what the extract suggests about how a craft is really learnt. Answer in about 120 words.

value_points: Thomas begins impatient, wanting to open every clock at once
Working beside Mr Elias, he learns to sit still, to wind, and to wait
He learns to listen for the small uneven heartbeat inside the brass case
The extract suggests a craft is learnt slowly, by watching, waiting, and paying attention
It also suggests the master's patience matters as much as the learner's effort

choice.alternative_prompt: Write a character sketch of Mr Elias in about 120 words, bringing out his skill, his patience, and his attitude towards his work.

questions.prompt: The extract ends with the words, 'The listening is everything.' Explain what 'listening' means here, with examples from the extract. Answer in about 120 words.

alternative_value_points: A master of his craft: forty years in the same shop, once steady enough to hold a screw the size of a grain of rice
Patient by principle: a clock tells you its fault if you have the patience to listen
His hearing has sharpened with age even as his hands tremble
Generous as a teacher: he passes his magnifying glass, and his philosophy, to Thomas
value_points: Listening means patient attention, not hearing with the ears alone
Mr Elias holds that a clock reveals its own fault to anyone patient enough to listen
Thomas learns the same lesson: to sit still, to wind, to wait, and to hear the heartbeat inside the case
The closing gift of the magnifying glass underlines that tools matter less than attention
